# ADAM on ARC-AGI-3:
self-evaluation and world-model learning report.

ARC-style interactive tasks are useful because they exercise world model, exploration, action, memory, and adaptation in one loop. We use them as an engineering gate for ADAM — not as a claim that AGI is solved.

Claim discipline. This is a non-official self-evaluation scorecard. It is not a Kaggle submission and not a leaderboard rank claim. We publish it because the cognitive-loop signal (world model + action + memory) is useful regardless of any official ranking.

## Why this matters, and what we are not claiming.

The useful signal is not a rank. The useful signal is that ADAM was put into interactive tasks where the same engine has to: build a model of the environment from scratch, decide what to try next, remember what already happened, and pursue goals over time. That is exactly the cognitive loop the engine is being engineered to close.

What we claim. ADAM reaches 73 of 183 levels (26.71%) with 1,393 actions across 3 of 25 public ARC-AGI-3 environments under an autonomous configuration. The scorecard is dated 2026-07-03 and the run is reproducible.

What we do not claim.

  * Not a Kaggle submission. Not a leaderboard rank claim. Not an "official ARC Prize" position.
  * Not a claim that ADAM is AGI or ASI. ADAM is on an AGI track and is not AGI today.
  * Not a "general intelligence solved" claim. ARC-AGI-3 is one behavioural gate, not the final answer.
  * Not a marketing "#1" line. The percentage is small and the work to close the loop is ongoing.

# Level Solver (`solver.html`, `src/solver.js`)

A standalone page that picks a level and tries to find a sequence of skill assignments that solves it, entirely off-DOM, then hands back a "Watch replay" link into the real `game.html`. It's a best-effort heuristic solver, not a guaranteed one — see Limitations below.

## Important notice

Lemmings is proven PSPACE-complete So there is no way to brute force a solution.

## How it operates, end to end

Picking a level in `solver.html` triggers `loadLevelDef` (the exact same level loader `game.html` itself uses) followed by `setupSolverWorld`, which bakes the level's terrain onto an `OffscreenCanvas`, builds a `trapTracker`, and takes one pristine snapshot of that empty-of-lemmings state (`world.baseSnapshot`) — this snapshot is the thing every subsequent simulation resets back to, so nothing ever contaminates anything else. Each max-uses field's preset is exactly what the currently-loaded level provides (`levelDef.lemmingTypes[job]`), not `defaultPolicy()`'s own generic defaults — `defaultPolicy()`'s build/block values (6/3) exist for programmatic callers with no specific level in hand yet (a conservative "don't blow every builder on the first gap" starting point); once a real level is loaded there's an actual number to show, and showing anything else read as simply wrong (a level handing out 99 builders showing a preset of "6" was reported as a bug — fixed by always seeding the field from the level's own count instead). Both the field's displayed value and its HTML `max` attribute update on every level load, so a level with e.g. only 1 miner shows "Max miner uses: 1", and a level with none of a job shows 0 — that job simply can't be requested for this level from the UI at all.

These fields become `solveLevel`'s `initialPolicyOverrides`, merged over `defaultPolicy()`'s own values (`{...defaultPolicy(), ...initialPolicyOverrides}`) to build the one fixed `policy` object the whole search uses.

  * Level preview: confirmed Solve starts disabled with no level picked; picking `fun/1` renders the correct title ("fun 1 — Just dig!"), stats ("Lemmings: 10 · Save: 1 · Time limit: 5:00"), a jobs list correctly showing only "Digger: 10" (the level's only nonzero skill, out of all 8), a real-sized preview canvas, and enables Solve; switching to `fun/2` updates the title; clearing the picker hides the preview and disables Solve again — all 12 Advanced/budget field labels (2 budget + 3 probe + 7 per-job caps, in the expected order) present throughout.
  * Per-job caps are genuinely enforced, not just accepted and ignored: setting "Max digger uses" to 0 on `fun/1` ("Just dig!", a digger-only level) made it fail to solve (0/1 saved across 20 attempts) where it otherwise solves instantly — confirming the cap flows from the UI field through `initialPolicyOverrides` into `tryAssignCapped`'s enforcement. A normal, uncapped solve immediately afterward on the same level still succeeded, confirming the already-loaded/cached `world` (passed to `solveLevel` via its `world` option to skip re-decoding) produces correct, working replay links same as before this pass.
  * Level-select + per-job cap auto-clamping: confirmed the picker renders 17 `<optgroup>`s (one per non-2-player rating) with real DOS names async- filled in ("1 — Just dig!"); confirmed the initially-selected level's preview auto-loads with no interaction; confirmed switching from `fun/1` to `fun/4` updates every "Max `<job>` uses" field's value AND `max` attribute to that level's own counts (climb: 999-sentinel → 10, mine: 999-sentinel → 1, everything the level provides none of → 0); confirmed Solve still worked correctly on `fun/1` under the new picker/defaults.

CHAPTER 3

Solving

Up to here, we have seen how to model a problem with the `Model` object. To solve it, we need to use the `Solver` object that is obtained from the model as follows:

```text
Solver solver = model.getSolver();
```

The `Solver` is in charge of alternating constraint-propagation with search, and possibly learning, in order to compute solutions. This object may be configured in various ways.

## 3.1 Core solving methods

### 3.1.1 Solution computation

#### Finding one solution

A call to `solver.solve()` launches a resolution which stops on the first solution found, if any:

```text
if(solver.solve()){
    // do something, e.g. print out variable values
}else if(solver.hasReachedLimit()){
    System.out.println("The solver could not find a solution
                      nor prove that none exists in the given limits");
}else {
    System.out.println("The solver has proved the problem has no solution");
}
```

If `solver.solve()` returns `true`, then a solution has been found and each variable is instantiated to a value. Otherwise, two cases must be considered:

- A limit has been declared and reached (`solver.hasReachedLimit()` returns true). There may be a solution, but the solver has not been able to find it in the given limit or there is no solution but the solver has not been able to prove it (i.e., to close to search tree) in the given limit. The resolution process stops in no particular place in the search tree.
- No limit has been declared or reached: The problem has no solution and the solver has proved it.

There are some problems with your query:

  * In Prolog you cannot write something like `D is D+1`, because a variable can only be assigned one value;
  * at the moment you call `D is D+1`, `D` is not yet instantiated, so it will probably cause an error; and
  * You never state (at least not in the visible code) that the `level/2` of the root is `0`.

A solution is to first state that the level of any root is `0`:
    
    Copy
    
    `level(N,0) :-
        root(N).
    `

Now we have to define the inductive case: first we indeed look for a parent using the `above/2` predicate. Performing a check that `N` is no `root/1` is not necessary strictly speaking, because it would conflict with the fact that there is an `above/2`. Next we determine the level of that parent `LP` and finally we calculate the level of our node by stating that `L is LP+1` where `L` is the level of `N` and `LP` the level op `P`:
    
    Copy
    
    `level(N,L) :-
        above(P,N),
        level(P,LP),
        L is LP+1.
    `

Or putting it all together:
    
    Copy
    
    `level(N,0) :-
        root(N).
    level(N,L) :-
        above(P,N),
        level(P,LP),
        L is LP+1.
    `

About `root/1`

Note that by writing `root/1`, you introduce data duplication: you can simply write:
    
    Copy
    
    `root(R) :-
        \+ above(_,R).
    `

To circumvent this problem, instead of being truly deleted instances are simply *dismissed*: by labeling them with *instantiation levels*⁴, at a given level *n* only instances whose level is at most *n − 1* are considered. This is done by using the term indexing from the SAT model and eliminating literals whose instantiation level is above the threshold. At each instantiation round, the *level* is defined as the current level plus one. At the beginning of the solving all clauses are assigned level 0, the starting value for the instantiation level. At the end of an instantiation round, the SAT solver is notified that at that point in the decision tree there was an instantiation, so that whenever there is a backtracking to a point before such a mark the instantiation level is decremented, at the same time that all instances which have participated in a conflict are promoted to “level 0”. This ensures that those instances will not be dismissed for instantiation, which somehow emulates clause deletion. With this technique, however, the ground solver will still be burdened by the spurious instances, but they also will not need to be regenerated in future instantiation rounds.
